Patient demographics:

  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Vignette:
David was twenty-four when the mugging occurred on a rain-dampened pier near the New England coast. He had been returning to the patrol boat with his gear bag slung over his shoulder when a sudden movement from a shadowed alcove produced the threat. He remembered the exact weight of the hand against his chest, the sharp intake of breath from a stranger’s face, and the heavy clatter of his own equipment hitting the wooden planks. He was thirty now, and though the years had passed, he still could not seem to put that frightening event into words. The experience sat in him as a dense, unlabelled mass, too substantial for language. When his partner, Elena, asked him to describe the incident, he would trace the edge of his coffee cup and fall silent, certain that forcing a narrative would distort the truth. Sometimes, when the moments of the mugging rose to the surface, David could recall them with precise detail. He would list the angle of the streetlamp, the direction of the wind, the texture of the rain on his collar. Yet as the sequence unfolded, a complete numbness settled over him, as if the events had happened to a stranger in a different life. The feeling of threat was absent; only the architecture of the moment remained. Other times, his memories arrived as fragmented pieces that did not fit together. A sudden image of the torn canvas of his gear bag would appear during a morning briefing, followed hours later by a disconnected flash of the robber’s scuffed boot, with no clear bridge between them. David moved through his days holding these floating fragments, aware of their presence but unable to weave them into a continuous thread. His work as a Coast Guard patrolman provided a structured rhythm, and the station’s concrete deck and weathered steel bulkheads became the specific setting where these memory qualities surfaced. During a routine morning inspection, when the station commander’s palm landed on his shoulder to steady a clipboard, David felt the exact pressure of the mugging. The sensation struck him without language, a nonverbal trigger that mirrored the original encounter. He did not step away, nor did he question the distance. The emotionless recall coexisted with the trigger, and the fragmented pieces coexisted with his daily duties. He simply noted the touch, accepted the memory, and continued his rounds. His relationship with Elena continued alongside these quiet displacements; she would sit across from him in the evening, watching him hold his silence, aware that his internal landscape occupied the same room as his external life. Over the months, the accumulated weight of the unlinked flashes and the steady numbness formed a consistent presence. David continued his patrols, maintained his routines, and responded to calls, yet he found himself unable to finally name the event. He had come to believe that the silence inside him was simply the space where the past waited, neither demanding attention nor receding completely. His reports to command were technically precise, yet they lacked the connective tissue that usually bound his experiences together. The Coast Guard vessel remained his primary environment, and the deck remained the place where the mugging’s physicality repeated itself, unmediated by explanation. He accepted this arrangement, letting the fragments and the numbness share the same ground without merging. It was the persistent weight of these disconnected memories, the quiet detachment during his own life, and the inability to finally put the frightening event into words that brought David to the clinic. He had come to believe that the unspoken mass might eventually crowd out the present, and he hoped to find a way to ground the pieces without losing his footing. Sitting in the therapist’s office, David looked at his hands, aware of the memory of the pier, the distance in his chest, and the unformed words hovering just below his tongue. He was ready to stop waiting for the pieces to align, even if he could not yet say what they would form.
